items.stem: How should user passwords be stored?

options.text: Hashed with a slow, salted password-hashing function
options.rationale: Correct: salted, slow hashing resists cracking and precomputation.

options.text: Encrypted and decrypted on every login
options.rationale: Reversible encryption keeps plaintext recoverable if keys leak.

options.text: In plain text for easy support
options.rationale: Plain text exposes all passwords on any breach.

options.text: With a single fast unsalted hash
options.rationale: Fast unsalted hashes are quickly cracked and allow precomputed attacks.

items.explanation: Correct: a salted, deliberately slow password hash is the right choice.

items.stem: Which TWO statements about symmetric and asymmetric cryptography are correct? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Symmetric encryption is efficient for bulk data
options.rationale: Correct: symmetric ciphers are fast for large volumes.
Correct: public keys can be shared openly, easing distribution.

options.text: Asymmetric encryption is ideal for encrypting huge files directly
options.rationale: Asymmetric is slow; it typically protects a symmetric key instead.

options.text: Symmetric keys can be published safely
options.rationale: A shared secret key must stay confidential.

items.explanation: Correct: symmetric is efficient for bulk data and asymmetric eases key distribution.

items.stem: Why does encryption alone not guarantee that a message was not altered?

options.text: Encryption protects confidentiality; integrity needs a MAC or signature
options.rationale: Correct: a separate mechanism is required to detect tampering.

options.text: Encrypted data cannot be changed at all
options.rationale: Ciphertext can still be modified; detection requires integrity checks.
Encryption and signing are distinct operations.

options.text: Integrity is only a concern for plaintext

items.explanation: Correct: integrity requires a MAC or signature in addition to encryption.
